successors.note: 1795: Kamehameha took Maui and Molokaʻi at the Battle of Kawela and Oʻahu at the Battle of Nuʻuanu (Unification of Hawaii page); the Kalanikūpule page says the sacrifice of Kalanikūpule ended the Kingdom of Maui.

rulers.name: Kahekili II
rulers.note: Succession table: Aliʻi nui of Maui 1765 - August 27, 1791 (the page does not explain that end date) and of Oʻahu 1783-1793; died July 1794 at Ulukou, Waikīkī (Unification page: 'In 1794, the aged Kahekili II died'). The reconquest of Maui in 1791 is on the Unification page.

rulers.name: Kalanikūpule
rulers.note: Infobox: Mōʻī of Maui 1794-1795 and ruler of Oʻahu 1793-1795; Kāʻeokūlani held Maui and Molokaʻi in 1794 until his death.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no Maui row). The Kahekili II page dates his Maui rule from 1765; the Kalanikūpule page says Kāʻeokūlani gained Maui, Lānaʻi and Molokaʻi in 1794, which is the realm read back. No page gives the extent before 1783 and no page gives an area; Maui Nui at the grid is about 85 km radius (the same stand-in as the Hawaiian Kingdom dossier).

New keyframe: Kahekili II was ruler of Oʻahu from 1783 (succession table) after Kahahana 'lost his life and his kingdom in the war with Maui in 1783' (Unification page). From 1790 to 1791 Kamehameha held Maui for a year (ledger contest); from July to December 1794 Maui and Molokaʻi are Kāʻeokūlani's (ledger).

ledger.note: 1765: Kahekili II becomes aliʻi nui of Maui. The succession table of the Kahekili II page lists 'Aliʻi nui of Maui 1765 - August 27, 1791'; the earlier kings of Maui and the extent of the kingdom are not on the pages opened, so the dossier starts at the first page-dated year of Kahekili's rule and the extent is the researcher's reading (Maui Nui).

1783: Kahekili II conquers Oʻahu. Kahahana, the last independent king of Oʻahu, 'lost his life and his kingdom in the war with Maui in 1783' (footnote of the Unification page); the Kahekili II page lists him as aliʻi nui of Oʻahu 1783-1793 after Kahahana.

1790: Kamehameha invades Maui. 'In 1790, while the aliʻi Kahekili II was on Oʻahu, Kamehameha's army invaded Maui' with John Young and Isaac Davis's help and defeated 'Maui's army led by Kahekili's son Kalanikūpule at the bloody Battle of Kepaniwai'.

1791: Kahekili retakes Maui. 'In 1791, Kahekili, supported by his brother Kāʻeokūlani, aliʻi of Kauaʻi, reconquered Maui' and gained cannons; in April or May 1791 he tried to invade Hawaiʻi island but was defeated in a naval battle at Kepuwahaʻulaʻula near Waipiʻo.

1794: Kahekili II dies and leaves Maui and Molokaʻi to Kāʻeokūlani. 'In 1794, the aged Kahekili II died' (July 1794 at Waikīkī, Kahekili II page), leaving Oʻahu to Kalanikūpule and Maui and Molokaʻi to Kāʻeokūlani, who was also aliʻi of Kauaʻi (page, paraphrased). The month is the death's; the bequest is undated within 1794.

1794: Kalanikūpule kills Kāʻeokūlani and holds Maui and Molokaʻi again. The Unification page: the civil war between Kalanikūpule and Kāʻeokūlani 'ended when Kalanikūpule killed Kāʻeokūlani'; the Kamakahelei page: Kāʻeokūlani was killed at the Battle of Kukiiahu on December 12, 1794 (closely paraphrased). The page does not link the two sentences; the Kalanikūpule page says Kamehameha took these islands from Kalanikūpule's rule 'in 1794' while the Unification page says 1795.

1795: Kamehameha takes Maui and Molokaʻi. 'in 1795, Kamehameha set sail with an armada of 960 war canoes and 10,000 soldiers' and quickly took Maui and Molokaʻi at the Battle of Kawela (the battle is undated within 1795 on the page).

1795: Oʻahu falls and the Kingdom of Maui ends. 'After his conquest of Oahu in the summer of 1795' Kamehameha prepared for Kauaʻi; the Battle of Nuʻuanu, where more than 700 men went over the Pali, is undated beyond this; Kalanikūpule was later captured and sacrificed to Kū-ka-ili-moku, which the Kalanikūpule page says ended the Kingdom of Maui.

wars.name: Kahekili's conquest of Oʻahu
wars.outcome: Kahahana, last independent king of Oʻahu, lost his life and his kingdom in 1783; Kahekili II ruled Oʻahu 1783-1793.
wars.note: The page gives the year in a footnote only; no battle is named.

wars.name: Kamehameha's invasion of Maui and Kahekili's reconquest
wars.outcome: Kamehameha won at Kepaniwai (1790); in 1791 Kahekili reconquered Maui and then lost the naval battle of Kepuwahaʻulaʻula (April or May 1791) off Waipiʻo.
wars.note: The Battle of ʻĪao is not on the page; Kepaniwai is the page's name for the 1790 fight.

wars.name: Kalanikūpule and Kāʻeokūlani's civil war
wars.outcome: Kāʻeokūlani was killed (the Kamakahelei page: Battle of Kukiiahu, 12 December 1794) and Kalanikūpule held Maui and Molokaʻi; the war also began a succession crisis on Kauaʻi.
wars.note: The Kalanikūpule page names the Battle of Kalauao and says Kalanikūpule's forces, with British and American sailors, defeated Kaeo's warriors; the pages do not reconcile the two battle names.

wars.name: Kamehameha's 1795 invasion
wars.outcome: Battle of Kawela (Maui, Molokaʻi) then Waiʻalae, Waikīkī and Nuʻuanu on Oʻahu in the summer of 1795; Kalanikūpule was captured and sacrificed.
wars.note: Kaʻiana defected to Kalanikūpule and was killed in the fighting.

certainty.note: Island chiefdoms: coasts exact, rule over each island contested in 1790-1791 and 1794.

notes: A state Cliopatria lacks; 'Kingdom of Maui' did not load as a Wikipedia article (URL_NOT_FOUND), so the dossier rests on the Kahekili II, Kalanikūpule and Unification pages, with no infobox, capital or area. Not on any page opened: the kings of Maui before Kahekili II (the dossier starts at the first page-dated year, 1765), the capital (Waikīkī is only Kahekili's place of death), the conquest of Molokaʻi, Kahekili's earlier reign over Maui before 1765, why the Kahekili II table ends his Maui term on 27 August 1791 (the Unification page has him reconquer Maui in 1791 and die in 1794). Oʻahu before 1783 (Kahahana) needs its own dossier: counterparts_needing_dossiers. The 1794 split is recorded as a loss to and a gain from 'kingdom-of-kauai' because the Unification page lists Kāʻeokūlani, aliʻi of Kauaʻi, as holding Kauaʻi and, in 1794, Maui and Molokaʻi. Lānaʻi and Kahoʻolawe are inside the Maui Nui stand-in. The Hawaiian Kingdom dossier (kingdom-of-hawai-i) records the 1795 acquisition from 'Kalanikūpule (Maui, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu)'; the slug of this dossier is the intended counterpart. Region names: radii as in kingdom-of-hawai-i (gazetteer_names_needed: Maui Nui, Oʻahu, Kauaʻi and Niʻihau as regions).
